newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Young Russian reformers to present plans to EBRD.
newsitem.headline: Young Russian reformers to present plans to EBRD.

text.p: Russia's young reformers, swept to power last month, will present their economic blueprint this weekend as bankers from the West and post-communist world gather in London.

The Russian presentation will be the central point of the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, set up in 1991 to help the former Soviet bloc nations rebuild their economies on a free market model.
Russia, which accounts for about one quarter of the EBRD's business, inevitably dominates the bank's meetings.

But this year bankers will be keen to hear what plans the young reformers have for the Russian economy, following their promotion to power by President Boris Yeltsin in the latest swing of the Kremlin political pendulum.
"We expect there's going to be a lot of interest in the Russian country presentation... The focus is going to be very much on Russia," said the EBRD's Moscow representative Lou Naumovski.

The two-day meeting officially starts on Monday, but a business forum during which the post-communist EBRD members have the chance to present their reform plans, begins on Saturday. The Russians speak on Sunday.
The high-powered Russian delegation is led by Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin.
Dubinin, a former acting finance minister, is a relative veteran compared with the young men promoted in the last month's government reshuffle.

He was appointed central bank chief in late 1995 but since then he has won respect in the West as an inflation fighter. Although older than many of the newly-appointed whizz-kinds, his reform credentials are good.

Dubinin knows first hand the consequences of lax monetary management: Yeltsin sacked him as acting fiannce minister in 1994 after a dive in the rouble's value which also cost a previous central bank chief his job.
His delegation to the EBRD meeting is studded with members of the new reformist government.
It includes First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin, an ally of economy chief Anatoly Chubais and until recently a top finance aide of Yeltsin.
Another Chubais ally in the team is former deputy economy minister, Sergei Vasilyev, now Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's deputy chief of staff.
Naumovski said the EBRD would not be announcing any major new deals for Russia at the meeting.

But, as the country which dominates the EBRD's balance sheet, Russia is likely to play a key role in the bilateral meetings on the fringe of the meeting where often more business is done than in the plenary sessions.
Several new Russian projects are going through the EBRD pipeline. One of the most high-profile is a $125 million syndicated loan for Russian gas monopoly Gazprom.
About 20 bankers visited Gazprom last week and syndication of the deal closed on Thursday. Naumovski said it was likely to be oversubscribed.
But the new Russian reformers say they want to tackle the powerful monopolies such as Gazprom, which they accuse of inefficiency and bad management.
TROUBLE-FREE TIES
Relations with the EBRD, which concentrates on the private sector, are probably the most trouble-free of Russia's ties with international financial institutions.
The International Monetary Fund has suspended payments on its $10 billion, three-year loan to Russia because tax revenues are running far below budgeted levels.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said in Moscow earlier this month that he was ready to recommend agreement on a 1997 programme for Russia, but there are no signs that a resumption of disbursing delayed money is imminent.

The World Bank acknowledges its Russian portfolio was one of its most troubled in early 1996. It has now removed many bottlenecks holding up disbursement of loans, but problems remain and benefits are not reaching the people.
World Bank president James Wolfensohn, now in Moscow for talks with leaders of the new cabinet, said this week his bank could lend Russia $9 billion over the next three years.
"The intent was to fly the flag and say that we're here to support structural reforms," World Bank Moscow chief economist Vladimir Konovalov said of the Wolfensohn visit.
The success of Russia's debut dollar Eurobond last year and its mark issue last month shows that it is not dependent on the international institutions alone for funds.
But their presence makes other investors feel comfortable and, as in its other client states, the EBRD sees one of its main roles as being a catalyst for additional, private-sector investment.
RUSSIA DOMINATES EBRD BUSINESS

Russian officials occasionally grumble about slow disbursement of EBRD deals. But the bank can pride itself on the rapid growth of business with Russia, which became a member only in 1992 after the break-up of the Soviet Union.
At the end of 1996 the EBRD had 450 projects in place, with 10 billion Ecu ($11.3 billion) of loans and investment approved, including $3 billion for Russia.
That figure has now risen to $3.5 billion, of which $2.5 billion has been signed and $1.0 billion disbursed. By value, 17 percent of projects are equity and the rest are debt.

With a network of regional venture capital funds spreading across the country, the EBRD now has at least one project in 50 of Russia's 89 regions. One of the funds, in Smolensk, will be fully invested by this summer.
The EBRD and World Bank have jointly set up a Financial Institutions Development Programme, to help the troubled banking sector and create a core of 30 or 40 strong banks.

Related to this programme, the EBRD has taken equity stakes in two institutions -- Tokobank and Avtobank -- and one smaller bank. It has also provided credit lines to Russian banks totalling $480 million, to be lent on to firms and institutions.
NO ROUBLE FUNDING
Bankers said the EBRD, which funds itself in a range of exotic currencies, Asian and African as well as East European, would love to pioneer foreign borrowing in the rouble debt market.
Moscow officials have spoken of the possibility of Russia issuing a rouble Eurobond, but bankers said they had so far blown cold on the idea of an EBRD rouble issue.
